analysis.one_liner: Makes it national law that government cannot deny or interfere with a woman's right to choose abortion.
analysis.headline: With 110 cosponsors from both parties, the bill was referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee in May 2007 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The Freedom of Choice Act would write the core of the Roe v. Wade ruling into federal statute: no federal, state, or local government could deny or interfere with a woman's decision to bear a child, end a pregnancy before fetal viability, or end one after viability to protect her life or health. It would apply to existing laws retroactively and let individuals sue in court to enforce the right. It died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who need or may need abortion care, especially those in states with heavy restrictions — 87 percent of U.S. counties already had no abortion provider when the bill was filed. Reproductive health clinics also benefit because the bill would strike state rules that limit their operations.

how_it_helps.text: Declares a national policy that every woman has a fundamental right to choose to bear a child, end a pregnancy before viability, or end one after viability when necessary for her life or health, and bars any federal, state, or local government from denying or interfering with that choice.

Prohibits governments from discriminating against the exercise of those rights in providing benefits, facilities, services, or information, and applies the protection retroactively to laws already on the books.
Lets any individual aggrieved by a violation sue in civil court to obtain relief, including against a government entity.

analysis.who_pays: No one pays a direct monetary cost. The parties that lose are state and local governments, which could no longer enforce waiting periods, consent rules, or bans the bill conflicts with, and opponents of abortion who lose the ability to restrict it through state law.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition reaches post-viability abortion whenever it is 'necessary to protect the life or health of the woman,' a health standard broader than Roe's, which critics said would allow late-term abortions in nearly all circumstances.
The bill applies retroactively and would wipe out state laws already in force — including waiting periods, informed-consent requirements, and bans — prompting a wave of litigation against states.
A statutory right enforceable through civil suits against governments would generate ongoing court challenges over what counts as 'interference' with the right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women who depend on abortion access, the bill converts a court-protected right into a statute that is harder to erode, which is its main value. The cost is real but falls on the regulatory side: it would invalidate a range of existing state abortion laws, including some with broad public support, and its broad health standard would permit abortions after viability in many circumstances. How one weighs this depends largely on one's view of abortion itself, but the bill's practical effect would be the most protective national abortion-access standard ever enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee in May 2007, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on April 19, 2007 with 110 original cosponsors — 108 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On May 4, 2007 the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action during the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that restrict abortion and the anti-abortion organizations that support those restrictions kept the status quo: no hearing was ever held, so no existing state law was ever threatened. Women in restrictive states got no new federal protection.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 110 original cosponsors.

for.name: 108 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, alongside 2 House Republicans.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction holding the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 4, 2007 and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote during the 110th Congress, despite a Democratic majority and more than 100 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: National Right to Life Committee
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the Freedom of Choice Act as a bill that would invalidate existing abortion restrictions.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 108 of the 110 cosponsors were House Democrats, with 2 Republicans joining. The Congress ended before any roll call could show how the full chamber might have split.

industries.industry: Reproductive health and abortion care providers
industries.note: The bill bars governments from interfering with the choice or discriminating in the provision of services, protecting clinic operations from state restrictions. Patients and providers benefit together, since access depends on clinics being able to operate.

industries.industry: Anti-abortion organizations and crisis pregnancy centers
industries.note: Retroactive application would invalidate state laws these groups lobbied for, including waiting periods and bans. Their interest in restricting the choice runs against the women who would use it.
States would lose authority to regulate abortion access, enforceable through private lawsuits against them. Governments lose power here rather than money.
